clue.text: Dear Dandelion, unusual Victorian novel

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters before it are put out of their usual order

blocks.note: the thirteen letters of these two words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A letter opening 'Dear Dandelion' would make for an odd Victorian novel.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's last completed book, published in 1876, is a famous work of nineteenth-century fiction.

clue.text: Risky opening with backgammon piece

blocks.note: a door is an opening into a room
a die is one of the dice thrown in backgammon

explanation.surface: A daring first move in a game of backgammon.
explanation.definitionFit: A do-or-die venture stakes everything on success, so it is a hazardous, all-or-nothing undertaking.

clue.text: Not a soul with energy after midday

indicators.note: after says the energy letter is placed behind the word for midday

blocks.note: midday is twelve noon
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone lacks any spirit or energy once lunchtime has passed.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean nobody at all; 'not a soul' is an idiom for the absence of any person.

clue.text: Artist's joy (mostly) rising about cobalt

indicators.note: mostly means not all of the word, so its final letter is dropped
in a down clue rising reads the word upwards, from bottom to top

blocks.note: glee is joy; without its last letter
re means about or concerning
Co is the chemical symbol for cobalt

explanation.surface: An artist's happiness grows as he works with cobalt blue.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay. EL GRECO was the Cretan-born painter of Toledo.
explanation.definitionFit: Domenikos Theotokopoulos, known by this nickname, was a Renaissance painter famous for elongated figures.

clue.text: As a product of Smith and Wesson might be?

definitions.text: As a product of Smith and Wesson might be?

blocks.clueFragment: As a product of Smith and Wesson might be?
blocks.note: surface reading: describing a firearm made by the American gun company
setter's reading: a child of a Smith and a Wesson might carry both family names joined by a hyphen

explanation.walkthrough: Smith & Wesson makes guns, some of which have two barrels; but a product of a Mr Smith and a Ms Wesson is their child, with a hyphenated surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The term describes both a shotgun with two barrels and a hyphenated two-part surname, often thought posh in Britain.

clue.text: Regret sports lesson, having torn around

indicators.note: around says the word for torn is wrapped about the lesson, holding it inside

blocks.note: rent is an old past participle of rend, meaning torn
PE is physical education, the school sports lesson

explanation.surface: A pupil regrets the games lesson after ripping their kit.
explanation.walkthrough: Rent, an old past form of rend, splits after its first two letters to take the lesson inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To repent is to feel sorrow or contrition for something done, a stronger synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Granny gets food, eating trout for starters somewhere in Massachusetts

indicators.note: starters are the opening letters, so the first letter of each of the two words is taken

blocks.note: nan is a familiar name for a grandmother
tuck is British school slang for food, especially sweets and snacks
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Grandma is served fish on a seaside holiday in New England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eating trout' looks like the fish going inside something, but the two words just supply their first letters. TUCK is the British schoolchild's word for snacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantucket is an island and town off Cape Cod, a place in that US state famed for whaling.

clue.text: Cab seen, unusually: it's a scarcity

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, taken as written

explanation.surface: Spotting a taxi is a rare event.
explanation.definitionFit: Absence can mean a lack or want of something, as in an absence of evidence, so a shortage.

clue.text: 'Well ... well ...'; that's indifferent

blocks.note: 'so' and 'well' are both fillers used to begin a remark
the same filler again

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates, saying 'well, well', which shows they are not impressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something only middling or mediocre is neither good nor bad, which is one meaning of indifferent.

clue.text: Irascibility shown by US solider eating steak on headland

indicators.note: eating takes food inside, so the soldier's letters enclose the steak
on means placed next to, so the headland word follows

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier
rump steak is a cut of beef
a ness is a promontory, as in Scottish place names

explanation.surface: An American soldier having steak on a clifftop is bad-tempered.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue prints 'solider', a typo for soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Grumpiness is crotchety bad temper, which is what irascibility means: being easily angered.

clue.text: Stick commercial in this place

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial or advertisement
here means in this place

explanation.surface: Pin an advert up here.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to cling or remain fixed to a surface, the verb sense of sticking.

clue.text: Unveiling – not very excitedly – some pasta

indicators.note: not says the following abbreviation is taken out of the first word
excited letters jump about, so what remains is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
v is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A chef calmly reveals a dish of pasta.
explanation.definitionFit: Linguine is a flat, ribbon-shaped Italian noodle, so one kind among many pastas.

clue.text: Sucks it up again, uneasily sore with barbs

indicators.note: uneasily suggests restless disorder, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone stung by sharp remarks takes the pain stoically yet again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucks it up' suggests putting up with hurt, but here it is literal soaking up.
explanation.definitionFit: To reabsorb is to take in a liquid once more, as a sponge or the body does.

clue.text: Invest in figurative painter that might come from Tamworth

blocks.note: to back a venture is to invest in it
Francis Bacon was a twentieth-century figurative painter

explanation.surface: A buyer is urged to put money into a representational artist from the Staffordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: A Tamworth is a British breed of pig, named after the Staffordshire town; back bacon is a lean cut of bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: Back bacon is cured pork, which could be produced from a Tamworth pig.

clue.text: Heaven's, they say, a Scottish island

indicators.note: they say points to how a word is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: heaven is the sky; with the possessive it is pronounced like the island

explanation.surface: People call a certain Scottish island heavenly.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is the largest of the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of the Highlands.

clue.text: Fire axe

blocks.note: first meaning: dismiss from a job
second meaning: also dismiss, or cut

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a firefighter's tool, but both words are verbs for dismissing staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Firing and axing are both informal verbs for removing an employee from their job.

clue.text: Struggled with piano replacing Latin quintet in bands

indicators.note: replacing says one letter takes another's place within the word

blocks.note: to strive is to struggle
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: A pianist had trouble joining a Latin music ensemble playing in groups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latin quintet' is not a band of five but the Roman numeral for five.
explanation.definitionFit: Striped means marked with stripes, that is with long narrow strips of colour.

clue.text: Fat ... warrior at heart ... criminal; a little celebrated in this country?

definitions.text: Fat ... warrior at heart ... criminal; a little celebrated in this country?

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so the middle letters of the word are kept
criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters are bent out of order
a little of a word is just its opening letter
in says one letter sits inside the country's abbreviation

blocks.note: taken as written
the central three letters of this word
for a British setter this country is the United Kingdom
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A portly fighter who is an outlaw at heart enjoys modest fame in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: Robin Hood's fat, fighting friar was an outlaw and is a celebrated English folk figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Friar Tuck is the stout, sword-wielding cleric of Robin Hood's band of outlaws in English legend.

clue.text: Scratching head, prejudiced craftsman

indicators.note: scratching means striking out, and the head is the first letter, so that letter goes

blocks.note: a partisan view is biased towards one side

explanation.surface: A biased tradesman scratches his head in puzzlement.
explanation.definitionFit: An artisan is a skilled manual worker who makes things by hand, a synonym for a craftsperson.

clue.text: On location for filming, 'attended' fictional court

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means sitting above, so the word for attended goes on top

blocks.note: came means turned up or attended
a film lot is the studio grounds where scenes are shot

explanation.surface: Someone turned up on a film set where an Arthurian court is being shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Camelot is the legendary seat of King Arthur and the Round Table, a castle and court of romance.

clue.text: Primarily, something African fauna adjudge 'really irritating'?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each following word is taken

blocks.note: opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter

explanation.surface: Wild animals in Africa find tourist trips a real nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as a playful description: an expedition that the lions and elephants might find a pest.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari is a trip to observe or hunt big game in Africa, which the animals themselves might resent.

clue.text: Writer not beginning to describe capture in game

indicators.note: not beginning means without its first letter
to describe is to draw around, as one describes a circle, so these letters enclose the next

blocks.note: a scribe is a writer
to bag is to capture, as a hunter bags game

explanation.surface: A novelist without an opening line writes about capture in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describe' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line around something.
explanation.definitionFit: Cribbage is a card game for two to four players, scored with pegs on a board.

clue.text: Heartless orc in long book, not present-day

indicators.note: heartless means the middle letter is removed
in says what remains is placed inside the book word

blocks.note: taken as written
a tome is a large, weighty book

explanation.surface: A goblin with no heart appears in a fantasy epic like Tolkien's.
explanation.definitionFit: Something yet to come lies in the future, so it does not belong to the current time.

clue.text: Oddly claim 'Hero's a small role'

indicators.note: oddly means the first, third, fifth and further odd-numbered letters are kept

blocks.note: the odd-placed letters of these two words run together

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that the hero's part is only a bit part.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameo is a brief appearance by a well-known actor in a play or film, a tiny part.

clue.text: Exhibitions, ones that impart finer vision

blocks.note: first meaning: grand displays or shows
second meaning: glasses worn to see better

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a roundabout description of eyeglasses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the plural of an impressive public show and also the name for a pair of glasses.

clue.text: Recalled Michelangelo mixing a little spot of pigment

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
a little means only a small part of the words is used

blocks.note: the end of the artist's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A painter recalls Michelangelo blending a dab of paint.
explanation.definitionFit: A mole is a small dark blemish on the skin caused by a cluster of pigmented cells.

clue.text: Small dog. Brown, perhaps. Conked out in French mountain

blocks.note: Dan Brown is the author of The Da Vinci Code
conked out is slang for died
taken as written
mont is French for mountain

explanation.surface: A little dog, perhaps brown, died on a mountain in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown' looks like the dog's colour but is a surname, so 'perhaps' points to a Brown, here novelist Dan.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dandie Dinmont is a short-legged Scottish Border terrier breed named after a Walter Scott character.
